title: Piedmont power line company wants to restrict hunting during environmental surveys
summary: The company planning a power line across northern Maryland wants a federal judge to restrict hunting by landowners on days when surveyors are doing their work, but property owners said they would not entertain such bans "even for a minute."
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters November 25, 2025

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters November 25, 2025

As he argued in Baltimore’s federal courthouse Tuesday, attorney Harris Eisenstein pulled a bright orange hunting vest from his bag and hoisted it into the air.

“This is all that it takes,” he said.

If power line surveyors from PSEG Renewable Transmission simply don the fluorescent orange and pink that hunters are well accustomed to, they won’t face any real danger completing environmental inspections in rural Maryland during hunting season, Eisenstein said.

PSEG, the company behind the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, a 67-mile transmission line planned through Baltimore, Carroll and Frederick counties, doesn’t think it’s quite so simple.

Surveyors for the proposed line could be crouched in the underbrush, rummaging about, making them difficult for hunters to see, even if they wore bright colors, said Kurt Fischer, an attorney representing PSEG.

The company is asking U.S. District Judge Adam B. Abelson to prevent landowners from hunting, or allowing hunting, on their property on any days when PSEG has indicated that it plans to come and survey — unless they contact the power company to request permission.

The landowners, who number in the hundreds, oppose any court-ordered hunting ban, “even for a minute,” Eisenstein said.

“They are creating a recipe for a tragedy,” Fischer said.

Abelson declined to rule immediately after Tuesday’s hearing, but acknowledged arguments on both sides: The surveyors have a right to enter private property to conduct their inspections, as required by the Maryland Power Plant Research Program, he said, but landowners have a right to hunt on their own land during the proper season.

US marshals won’t be used for protection during Maryland power line surveys — for now

“What we have are competing rights,” Abelson said Tuesday. “I’m trying to put these competing rights together and find a reasonable solution.”

Attorneys representing several hundred landowners proposed that PSEG give 72 hours notice of survey activities during any Maryland hunting season, and provide specific details about their activities so hunters can prepare for their arrival. That, in addition to requiring that surveyors wear the bright-colored gear.

The two sides were in the same courtroom in May, when the power company and the landowners sparred over whether the court could require property owners to allow the surveys over their objections.

Abelson concluded in June that PSEG has the authority to complete the surveys, which will ultimately inform the Maryland Public Service Commission’s decision whether or not to allow construction on the power line to begin. The landowners have appealed his ruling to the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

On Tuesday, Abelson gave PSEG that same authority over a third group of landowners, over protests from their attorneys, who said new information has emerged since Abelson’s June ruling, calling into question the urgency of the power company’s requests for land access.

Namely, the PSC issued a procedural schedule in September saying it will not make a final decision on the power line until February 2027, at the earliest. PSEG had said it needed surveying authority to meet a deadline from power system regulators to have the line in service by June 1, 2027.

“Their … application is stuck in the mud no matter what happens in this case,” Eisenstein said.

Despite the new PSC schedule, power company attorney Emily Wilson said time “very much remains of the essence here,” citing a letter from regional electric grid operator PJM Interconnection that calls for the line to be placed in service as soon as possible to avoid possibile grid failures.

Review for Piedmont power line will take until at least February 2027, Maryland regulators say

Eisenstein also argued that PSEG will need to conduct geotechnical boring surveys, but Maryland law does not allow it to compel that more invasive surveying, making it unlikely the company can meet its obligations.

Wilson argued that the Maryland Power Plant Research Program could determine that the geotechnical surveys are not necessary. Whether they are or not, it doesn’t change the fact that state law is on PSEG’s side with regard to property access, she said.

“What this case is focused on is the land access,” she said. “They do not have a right to exclude the company in this way.”

David Wyand, another attorney for the landowners, argued that the legislature only gave eminent domain powers to companies that have already been granted permission to construct their line. Technically, a state government entity, such as the Maryland Power Plant Research Program, could conduct the surveys, Wyand said, but PSEG can’t — as a private company.

“The General Assembly has specifically not said that PSEG has that right,” Wyand said.

But Abelson said that none of the new information changed his mind that PSEG should be able to collect its survey data, unimpeded by the landowners who disagree.

It’s unclear whether landowners will sway Abelson on the hunting issue, which they argue is urgent. Maryand’s firearm season for white-tailed deer, for instance, begins Saturday, and runs until Dec. 13.

Matt Moran, an Adamstown landowner in the path of the power line, said after Tuesday’s hearing that he recently received a notice from PSEG advising him that it plans to survey in the weeks ahead. If Abelson rules that landowners cannot hunt on any day when PSEG might  survey, Moran said he would only have one day open to hunt.

– Harris Eisenstein, attorney for Maryland landowners, of New Jersey-based PSEG

“That leaves me with one day to go out and get the venison that I need to feed my family, because I rely on venison to feed my family,” Moran said. “If you look in the freezer at my home, you’ll see that there’s more venison than there is beef, pork, chicken and fish combined.”

Attorneys for the landowners argued that hunting is not just a valued pastime for many rural Marylanders, but a relied-upon method for gathering food and reducing the number of animals that eat their crops.

“They are out-of-state,” Eisenstein said of New Jersey-based PSEG. “And they are out of touch.”

Eisenstein said PSEG’s practice of sending one notice to warn landowners about “multiple weeks” of surveying, even though actual surveys may only occur on particular days, “cloud” landowners’ lives. PSEG’s proposed hunting order could restrict the activity for weeks at a time, infringing on hunters’ rights, Eisenstein said.

PSEG’s attorneys argued that the company routinely coordinates with landowners who call with concerns about specific days, and that the company would “ideally” be able to come to agreement with landowners regarding hunting days.

But not all landowners are willing to work with PSEG. Some will not even correspond with the company, Wilson said. On at least one occasion, a landowner referenced hunting season in a Facebook post that PSEG perceived as a threat.

“We need that protection in place to protect our surveyors and their assistants,” Wilson said, “so that a really unfortunate accident does not occur.”

Wilson argued that Abelson needs to universally bar hunting during the survey work, and allow exceptions for particular properties. Eisenstein countered that hunting bans should be the exception — not the rule.

Nancy Gardetto, owner of Copper Penny Farm in Adamstown, said she, her husband and their two children are eagerly awaiting Saturday’s opening of deer season, which they also use to stock their freezers with venison, and cut down on the deer population to protect crops.

Gardetto also got a surveying notice from PSEG overlapping with the weeks of the hunt. She said she called PSEG to advise the company that it should not survey her property during that period because there would be hunting, and she feels the company should oblige. She made sure to emphasize that she was not making a threat, she said.

“They claim to have great coordination with all the property owners,” Gardetto said. “If that’s the case, I don’t understand why we need to ask permission to hunt our own farmland. I don’t understand why they can’t contact us and say: ‘Hey, we’ve got guys coming out tomorrow. Is anybody going to be there hunting?’”

“I don’t know why we had to be dragged into court to be forced into this,” Gardetto said.
